questions.title: Aero Baking Chocolate — Weights, Fractions, Volume and Recipe Conversions

subQuestions.questionText: An 'Aero for baking' chocolate slab weighs 175 g. Convert the full weight of the chocolate slab to kilograms.
subQuestions.memoText:
175 g ÷ 1 000 = 0,175 kg

Mark 1: dividing by 1 000
Mark 2: answer 0,175 kg

subQuestions.questionText: The 175 g slab is divided into 7 equal premeasured bars. How many grams does each bar of the chocolate slab measure?
subQuestions.memoText:
175 g ÷ 7 = 25 g per bar

Mark 1: dividing 175 g by 7
Mark 2: answer 25 g

subQuestions.questionText: What fraction of the full chocolate slab does one bar (25 g of 175 g) of the chocolate slab make?
subQuestions.memoText:
25/175 = 1/7

Mark 1: writing the fraction 25/175
Mark 2: simplifying to 1/7

subQuestions.questionText: Write the fraction from Question 1.1.3 (1/7) as a percentage, rounded off to one decimal place.
subQuestions.memoText:
1/7 × 100 = 14,285… = 14,3%

Mark 1: × 100
Mark 2: rounding to one decimal place → 14,3%

subQuestions.questionText:
Match the visual instructions (A to F) to each written instruction for making Aero Chocolate Fudge:
1. Collect and measure out one slab of 'Aero for Baking' (175 g) and one cup of cream.
2. Place the ingredients in a heat-resistant dish.
3. Heat the ingredients over a low heat until the mixture is melted and mixed together.
4. Pour the mixture into a 22 cm by 22 cm baking tin.
5. Spread and level the mixture into the baking tin and place in the fridge until cooled and solid.
6. Once the mixture has cooled, cut the Aero Chocolate Fudge and enjoy.
subQuestions.memoText:
1 → E
2 → D
3 → B
4 → F
5 → A
6 → C

[Award 1 mark per correct match]

subQuestions.label: 1.2.2 (a)
subQuestions.questionText: The cake tin is 22 cm by 22 cm by 5 cm. Calculate the volume of 1/3 of the cake tin, giving the solution to the nearest 10. Use: Volume = (1/3) × 22 × 22 × 5.
subQuestions.memoText:
= (1/3) × 22 × 22 × 5
= (1/3) × 2 420
= 806,6666…
≈ 810 cm³

Mark 1: substituting into the formula
Mark 2: 806,67
Mark 3: rounding to the nearest 10 → 810 cm³

subQuestions.label: 1.2.2 (b)
subQuestions.questionText: The correct unit of measurement for volume is:
subQuestions.memoText:
C — cm³

(Volume is measured in cubic units.)

[Award 2 marks for identifying option C]

subQuestions.label: 1.2.2 (c)
subQuestions.questionText: Would a cake baked in the 22 cm by 22 cm cake tin fit in a box with dimensions 7,5 inches by 7,5 inches? Complete the calculation, using 1 inch = 2,54 cm, and state whether the cake WILL or WILL NOT fit.
subQuestions.memoText:
7,5 inches × 2,54 cm = 19,05 cm
19,05 cm is less than 22 cm, so the cake WILL NOT fit in a 7,5 × 7,5 inch box.

Mark 1: 7,5 × 2,54
Mark 2: 19,05 cm
Mark 3: correct conclusion — WILL NOT fit

subQuestions.questionText: A no-bake cheesecake recipe uses 2 tbsp boiling water. If one tablespoon (tbsp) = 15 mℓ and one teaspoon (tsp) = 5 mℓ, calculate how many teaspoons of boiling water is needed for this recipe.
subQuestions.memoText:
2 × 15 mℓ = 30 mℓ
30 mℓ ÷ 5 mℓ = 6 teaspoons

Mark 1: 2 × 15 mℓ
Mark 2: ÷ 5 → 6 teaspoons

subQuestions.questionText: If 155 g = 3/4 cup of castor sugar, determine how many grams are in one cup.
The recipe requires 7 × 40 g packets of Aero Peppermint bar. What is the total amount (in grams) of Aero Peppermint bar required?
subQuestions.memoText:
7 × 40 g = 280 g

Mark 1: 7 × 40
Mark 2: answer 280 g

subQuestions.questionText: One 180 g packet of Crunchy Chocolate Balls Milk Chocolate contains 15 chocolate balls. What does each chocolate ball weigh?
subQuestions.memoText:
180 g ÷ 15 = 12 g each

Mark 1: dividing 180 g by 15
Mark 2: answer 12 g

questions.title: Mountain Biking — Wheel Circumference, Cog Ratios, Speed and Angles

subQuestions.questionText: A mountain bike wheel has a diameter of 66 cm, shown by the orange arrow labelled A. State the radius of the wheel in cm.
subQuestions.memoText:
Radius = 66 cm ÷ 2 = 33 cm

Mark 1: dividing the diameter by 2
Mark 2: answer 33 cm

subQuestions.questionText: Determine the distance (in metres, to 7 significant figures) a mountain bike can travel on one rotation of the wheel. Use: Distance of ONE rotation = 2 × 3,142 × radius, with radius = 33 cm = 0,33 m.
subQuestions.memoText:
Distance = 2 × 3,142 × 0,33
= 2,073720 m

Mark 1: converting the radius to 0,33 m
Mark 2: 2 × 3,142
Mark 3: × 0,33
Mark 4: answer 2,073720 m

subQuestions.questionText: A cyclist will travel 21,2 km on his mountain bicycle. Determine how many times the wheel would rotate to complete this trip. (One rotation covers 2,073720 m.)
subQuestions.memoText:
21,2 km = 21 200 m
Number of rotations = 21 200 ÷ 2,073720 = 10 224 turns

Mark 1: converting 21,2 km to 21 200 m
Mark 2: dividing by the distance per rotation
Mark 3: 10 223,9…
Mark 4: answer ≈ 10 224 rotations

subQuestions.label: 2.1.4 (a)
subQuestions.questionText: The small cog has 34 teeth and the large cog has 51 teeth. Write the ratio of the number of teeth on the small cog to the number of teeth on the big cog in simplest unit form.
subQuestions.memoText:
34 : 51
Divide both by 17
= 2 : 3

Mark 1: 34 : 51
Mark 2: simplified ratio 2 : 3

subQuestions.label: 2.1.4 (b)
subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the minimum number of rotations the small cog (34 teeth) and the large cog (51 teeth) must each make to line the two cogs back up in the exact position they were in when the rotation started (point A lines up with point B).
subQuestions.memoText:
Multiples of 34: 34; 68; 102; 136; …
Multiples of 51: 51; 102; 153; …
The lowest common multiple = 102 teeth.
Small cog: 102 ÷ 34 = 3 rotations
Large cog: 102 ÷ 51 = 2 rotations

Mark 1: multiples of 34
Mark 2: multiples of 51
Mark 3: LCM = 102
Mark 4: 3 rotations on the small cog and 2 rotations on the large cog

subQuestions.questionText: A graph of a short section of the Cederberg Mountain Bike Route shows the cyclist's speed over four consecutive 500 m segments as 28 km/h, 12 km/h, 48 km/h and 28 km/h. Determine the average speed this cyclist cycles to complete this section of the route.
subQuestions.memoText:
Average speed = (28 + 12 + 48 + 28) ÷ 4
= 116 ÷ 4
= 29 km/h

Mark 1: adding the four speeds
Mark 2: ÷ 4
Mark 3: answer 29 km/h

subQuestions.questionText: Complete the calculations to show how long it would take the cyclist to cycle the first 500 m at 28 km/h. Time = 500 m ÷ 28 km/h = ______ km ÷ 28 km/h = ______ hours = ______ hours ______ minutes.
subQuestions.memoText:
= 0,5 km ÷ 28 km/h
= 0,017857142 hours
= 0 hours 1 minute (≈ 1,07 minutes)

Mark 1: converting 500 m to 0,5 km
Mark 2: ÷ 28
Mark 3: 0,0178… hours
Mark 4: ≈ 0 hours 1 minute

subQuestions.questionText: The section shown on the graph covers four 500 m segments at 28, 12, 48 and 28 km/h. The whole 21,2 km route takes an average of 5 hours and 4 minutes. Calculate what fraction of the total length of time of this route is taken up during the section shown on the graph.
subQuestions.memoText:
Time per segment (in minutes):
0–500 m: 0,5 ÷ 28 h = 1,07 min
500–1 000 m: 0,5 ÷ 12 h = 2,5 min
1 000–1 500 m: 0,5 ÷ 48 h = 0,625 min
1 500–2 000 m: 0,5 ÷ 28 h = 1,07 min
Total for the section ≈ 5,265 minutes
Total route time = 5 h 4 min = 304 minutes
Fraction = 5,265 ÷ 304 = 1053/60 800 ≈ 0,0173

Mark 1–4: time for each of the four segments
Mark 5: total section time ≈ 5,265 min and total route time = 304 min
Mark 6: fraction 5,265 ÷ 304 (≈ 1053/60 800)

subQuestions.questionText: When riding downhill, the cyclist looks down, creating an angle labelled θ. Using the protractor shown in the image, measure the angle labelled θ.
subQuestions.memoText:
θ = 40°

[Award 2 marks for a correct reading (accept a small tolerance either side of 40°)]

questions.title: Soup Kitchen — Floor Plan Area, Temperature Conversion, Packing and Pot Volume

subQuestions.questionText: Study the floor plan for a soup kitchen. What is represented on the floor plan by the symbol at A?
subQuestions.memoText:
An oven (or stove).

[Award 2 marks]

subQuestions.questionText: The kitchen on the floor plan measures 22 feet by 37 feet. If one foot = 30,48 cm, determine the floor area (in m²) of the kitchen.
The walk-in cooler should be kept between 35 °F and 45 °F. Using the formula °F = 1,8 °C + 32, convert 35 °F to °C.
subQuestions.memoText:
35 = 1,8 °C + 32
35 − 32 = 1,8 °C
3 = 1,8 °C
°C = 3 ÷ 1,8 = 1,667 °C

Mark 1: subtracting 32 from both sides
Mark 2: dividing by 1,8
Mark 3: answer ≈ 1,67 °C

subQuestions.questionText: A donation of 144 Tomato & Onion Mix tins is given to the soup kitchen. Each storage shelf is 70 cm long, 30 cm deep and 37 cm high (usable space). Each tin is about 8,5 cm in diameter and 9,7 cm high. Show that the donation will fill 2 shelves if the tins are packed in neatly stacked rows.
subQuestions.memoText:
Along the length: 70 ÷ 8,5 = 8,235 → 8 tins
Along the depth: 30 ÷ 8,5 = 3,529 → 3 tins
Stacked in height: 37 ÷ 9,7 = 3,81 → 3 tins high
Tins per shelf = 8 × 3 × 3 = 72 tins
Two shelves = 72 × 2 = 144 tins
Therefore the donation of 144 tins will exactly fill 2 shelves.

Mark 1–2: 8 tins along the length
Mark 3: 3 tins along the depth
Mark 4: 3 tins high (stacked)
Mark 5–6: 8 × 3 × 3 = 72 tins per shelf
Mark 7: × 2 shelves = 144
Mark 8: conclusion — the donation fills exactly 2 shelves

subQuestions.questionText: A large soup pot has an outside diameter of 41 cm and an inside diameter of 40 cm. Calculate the thickness of the metal side of the pot.
subQuestions.memoText:
Thickness = (41 cm − 40 cm) ÷ 2 = 1 ÷ 2 = 0,5 cm

Mark 1: 41 − 40
Mark 2: dividing by 2 (a wall on each side)
Mark 3: answer 0,5 cm

subQuestions.questionText: The pot has an inside diameter of 40 cm and a height of 27 cm. By calculating the volume of the pot, determine how many bowls of soup can be served from such a pot. Use: Volume of a cylinder = 3,142 × radius × radius × height; each soup bowl contains 400 mℓ; 1 cm³ = 1 mℓ.
subQuestions.memoText:
Inside radius = 40 ÷ 2 = 20 cm
Volume = 3,142 × 20 × 20 × 27
= 33 933,6 cm³
= 33 933,6 mℓ
Number of bowls = 33 933,6 ÷ 400
= 84,8205
= 84 full bowls of soup

Mark 1: radius = 20 cm
Mark 2: substituting into the volume formula
Mark 3: 33 933,6 cm³
Mark 4: cm³ = mℓ
Mark 5: ÷ 400
Mark 6: 84 bowls (rounded down)

subQuestions.questionText: Each pot serves 84 bowls of soup. How many FULL pots of soup must be cooked to help 240 people (one bowl each)?
subQuestions.memoText:
240 ÷ 84 = 2,857
So 3 full pots must be cooked.

Mark 1: 240 ÷ 84
Mark 2: 2,857
Mark 3: rounding up → 3 full pots

questions.title: Hot-Air Ballooning — Probability Scale, Map Reading, Rates and Temperature

subQuestions.questionText: A May weather forecast can only be one of four types: Sunny (probability 1/2), Partially Cloudy (probability 1/5), Cloudy, or Rainy. The probabilities for Cloudy and Rainy are missing. If the probability for rain is double that of cloudy, determine the probability of the two missing weather forecasts (Cloudy and Rainy) as percentages.
subQuestions.memoText:
Let Cloudy = x, so Rainy = 2x.
1/2 + x + 1/5 + 2x = 1
3x = 1 − 1/2 − 1/5 = 3/10
x = 1/10 = 0,1
Cloudy = x = 10%
Rainy = 2x = 20%
(OR 100% − 50% − 20% = 30%; Cloudy = 30% ÷ 3 = 10%; Rainy = 20%.)

Mark 1: setting up the equation with x and 2x
Mark 2: 3x = 3/10
Mark 3: Cloudy = 10%
Mark 4: Rainy = 20%

subQuestions.questionText: Illustrate the probabilities of the four weather forecasts on a probability scale (from 0 to 1) by marking A for Sunny, B for Cloudy, C for Partially Cloudy and D for Rainy. State where each letter goes.
subQuestions.memoText:
A (Sunny) at 0,5 (1/2)
B (Cloudy) at 0,1 (1/10)
C (Partially Cloudy) at 0,2 (1/5)
D (Rainy) at 0,2 (2/10) — B, C and D all sit near the low end, with C and D together at 0,2.

Mark 1: A at 0,5
Mark 2: B at 0,1
Mark 3: C at 0,2
Mark 4: D at 0,2

subQuestions.questionText: A map shows the area around Parys in the Free State and a section of the Vaal River. Which province lies north of this section of the Vaal River?
subQuestions.memoText:
North West

[Award 2 marks for reading the map correctly]

subQuestions.questionText: Which national road runs from Kroonstad to Johannesburg?
subQuestions.memoText:
The N1

[Award 2 marks]

subQuestions.questionText: If a hot-air balloon rises at 2,4 m/sec, how high will the balloon be in 5 seconds?
subQuestions.memoText:
Height = 2,4 m/sec × 5 sec = 12 m

Mark 1: 2,4 × 5
Mark 2: answer 12 m

subQuestions.questionText: Kate dropped her camera from the balloon at a height of 92,4 m. The camera hits the ground after 6 seconds. A spectator, 10 m away from the balloon, starts to run at a constant speed of 2 metres per second as the camera starts to fall. Will he be able to reach the camera before it strikes the ground?
subQuestions.memoText:
Time for the spectator to cover 10 m = 10 m ÷ 2 m/sec = 5 seconds
The camera takes 6 seconds to fall.
5 seconds < 6 seconds, so yes — the spectator reaches the landing spot before the camera hits the ground.

Mark 1: 10 ÷ 2
Mark 2: = 5 seconds
Mark 3: comparing 5 s to 6 s and concluding 'yes'

subQuestions.questionText: The pilot told Kate that the tether line was 12 times his height, and that he was 1,9 m tall. How high did the hot-air balloon's tether line reach into the air?
subQuestions.memoText:
Tether line = 1,9 m × 12 = 22,8 m

Mark 1: 1,9 × 12
Mark 2: correct multiplication
Mark 3: answer 22,8 m

subQuestions.questionText: The radius of the hot-air balloon is 9 m at its widest point. How wide is the balloon?
subQuestions.memoText:
Width (diameter) = 9 m × 2 = 18 m

Mark 1: × 2
Mark 2: answer 18 m

subQuestions.questionText: Kate's ride lasted one and a quarter hours. How many minutes was her ride?
subQuestions.memoText:
1¼ hours × 60 = 75 minutes

Mark 1: 1,25 × 60
Mark 2: answer 75 minutes

subQuestions.questionText: The air in a typical hot-air balloon may be heated to 100 °C above ambient temperature. If the temperature on the day of Kate's flight was 23 °C, calculate the maximum temperature the hot-air balloon may be heated to.
subQuestions.memoText:
Maximum temperature = 23 °C + 100 °C = 123 °C

Mark 1: adding 100 °C
Mark 2: answer 123 °C

subQuestions.questionText: The formula to convert °C to °F is °F = (9/5)(°C) + 32 or °F = 1,8(°C) + 32. Write 1,8 as an equivalent fraction of 9/5 to show that these two formulas are the same.
subQuestions.memoText:
9/5 = 18/10 = 1,8
So 9/5 and 1,8 are the same value, which means the two formulas are the same.

Mark 1: 9/5 = 18/10
Mark 2: = 1,8

questions.title: Charly's Bakery — Scale Drawing, Probability Tree and Cape Town Street Maps

subQuestions.questionText: A 'koekie' (biscuit) is 12 cm by 12 cm in size. Describe the scale drawing of the koekie you would make using a scale of 1 : 3.
subQuestions.memoText:
Scaled length = 12 cm ÷ 3 = 4 cm
Draw a square 4 cm by 4 cm.

Mark 1: 12 ÷ 3
Mark 2: a 4 cm by 4 cm square

subQuestions.questionText: A mixed box of treats contains 4 koekies, 6 cupcakes and 2 petit fours (12 treats in total). If Amy-May picked one product from the box without looking, what is the percentage probability that she would pick a cupcake?
On the tree diagram, on the first branch (a koekie was picked first), the probability of picking a koekie as the second treat is 3/11. Explain why.
subQuestions.memoText:
One koekie has already been taken out of the box, so only 3 koekies are left, and only 11 treats remain in total. Therefore P(koekie second) = 3/11.

Mark 1: 3 koekies left
Mark 2: 11 treats left in total

subQuestions.questionText: Show how the probability of picking two koekies in succession (without replacement) was calculated.
A map of Cape Town's City Centre is given. How many tourist landmarks are depicted on the map?
subQuestions.memoText:
2 (accept 3)

[Award 2 marks for reading the map]

subQuestions.questionText: Which tourist landmark lies in a Northeasterly direction from Charly's Bakery?
subQuestions.memoText:
The Castle of Good Hope

[Award 2 marks]

subQuestions.questionText: On the zoomed-in street map, what street is Charly's Bakery in (point B)?
subQuestions.memoText:
Canterbury Street

[Award 2 marks]

subQuestions.questionText: How many restaurants are depicted on the street map?
subQuestions.memoText:
4 (accept 5 or 6, depending on how the map symbols are counted)

[Award 2 marks]

subQuestions.label: 5.4.3 (a)
subQuestions.questionText: Amy-May was dropped off at point A and walked along the sidewalk to Charly's Bakery (point B). Which street would Amy-May have to cross while on her way to Charly's Bakery?
subQuestions.memoText:
Constitution Street

[Award 2 marks]

subQuestions.label: 5.4.3 (b)
subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the distance Amy-May has to walk from A to B using the bar scale provided on the map. (On the map, the bar scale is about 1,5 cm to 20 m, and the route measures about 9,2 cm.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Distance = (route length ÷ bar-scale length) × 20 m
= (9,2 ÷ 1,5) × 20
= 122,67 m
(Using the larger map version: (13,8 ÷ 2,3) × 20 = 120 m.)
Answer ≈ 120 m.

Mark 1: measuring the bar scale (≈ 1,5 cm : 20 m)
Mark 2: measuring the route (≈ 9,2 cm)
Mark 3: dividing and multiplying by 20
Mark 4: answer ≈ 120 m

subQuestions.label: 5.4.3 (c)
subQuestions.questionText: Google Maps says Amy-May is 120 m from Charly's Bakery. Show that if she walked at a speed of 0,24 km/h and she was dropped off at 12:10, she would arrive at Charly's Bakery by 12:40.
subQuestions.memoText:
120 m = 0,12 km
Time = distance ÷ speed = 0,12 km ÷ 0,24 km/h = 0,5 hours = 30 minutes
12:10 + 30 minutes = 12:40 ✓

Mark 1: converting 120 m to 0,12 km
Mark 2: 0,12 ÷ 0,24
Mark 3: 0,5 hours = 30 minutes
Mark 4: 12:10 + 30 min = 12:40

subQuestions.questionText: Amy-May was given these directions to the Parliament building: outside Charly's Bakery, face south-east; turn right and follow a south-westerly direction along Canterbury Street; turn right onto Constitution Street; at the T-junction turn left onto Harrington Street; turn right in a north-westerly direction at the next road; continue half-way up the second block to reach the destination. Describe how you would illustrate these instructions on the map.
subQuestions.memoText:
Trace the route: start at Charly's Bakery facing south-east, turn right onto Canterbury Street heading south-west, turn right into Constitution Street, turn left at the T-junction onto Harrington Street, turn right (north-west) at the next road, and end half-way up the second block at the Parliament building.

Mark 1: correct start and first turn onto Canterbury Street (south-west)
Mark 2: right into Constitution Street
Mark 3: left onto Harrington Street at the T-junction
Mark 4: right (north-west) at the next road
Mark 5: ending half-way up the second block at Parliament
